> // Don't call memcpy on a potential nullptr dest

I guess it's `nullptr` `src` (zero size `data` → null `data.ptr()`), not `dest` (it was checked for on line 213). Calling `memcpy` with zero `count` is not UB, but calling it with `nullptr` `dest` or `src` is.
Not sure what can be `nullptr` in this case, `data.ptrw()` should never be `nullptr`, and `p_src` is checked before.

The check above is: `ERR_FAIL_COND_V(!p_src && p_length > 0, false);` 

"If not p_src *and* p_length >0" this means that if p_src == nullptr we still hit the memcpy, but only if p_length == 0. Calling memcpy with a null dest or src causes UB, even with a length of 0.
See my next comment. This is the same case.

> If not p_src and p_length > 0

Ah, indeed, I missed `p_length` part. But still, something like `if (ptr && p_src)` might be cleaner than checking size.

Neither data nor p_src are guaranteed to not be nullptr. if p_length ==0 it is likely because p_src is null, which is a case this code explicitly supports.

if p_length == 0 and pos == 0 then BOTH p_src and data.ptrw() will be nullptr. 

We would literally end up calling `memcpy(nullptr, nullptr, 0);`
At least in C, this situation now is well defined in latest standard, https://developers.redhat.com/articles/2024/12/11/making-memcpynull-null-0-well-defined#
We currently use c++17 where it is not, this pattern leads to actual non-theoretical crashes right now, see https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/100422 for instance.
The comment talks about checking the ptr, but you check the size instead. p_dst is already checked and an adress won't be null ?
Maybe have an assert to check length is less than 2^32 ? One day, someone will try to save a 4gb unicode file!
`constexpr const static ID INVALID_ID = -1;` ?
maybe check the last bit of integer ? If it is set, you'll overflow by casting to int64_t
`int64_t(integer) * -1;` uint64_t of -1 is setting all bits, i'm not sure that's what you want ?

This code is apparently very confusing. But p_dst has not been checked: 

`ERR_FAIL_COND_V(!p_dst && p_length > 0, -1);`

This code wants to support writing to a null pointer with a 0 length.
That is a good improvement
It is, I wrote it like this to make it clear that we are just flipping the sign.

That's what I meant by my previous comment, checks are logically fine, but comment is not clear. Changing the check to `if (src && dst)` will work the same, but it unambiguously shows what's checked, no comments needed.

> Ah, indeed, I missed p_length part. But still, something like if (ptr && p_src) might be cleaner than checking size.
I didn't want to make the check more expensive than necessary. But if a more expensive check, but no comment is preferred I can do that.

That won't work because we just add up the "positive part", so we will end up with just an int `10` and then we need to flip that sign. We don't do anything with the `-` at the start of the string except noting it.
`const T&` ?
maybe constexpr or define INT64_MAX / 10 to force it compile time ? The chance that it is not already are very slim but ...
This will definitely be constant folded by the compiler I don't think we need to do this explicitly.
Good catch!
`utf8.length() ` returns an signed int. If this changes this will generate a new compiler warning.
I could do a not +1 to flip it also, but that is almost certainly what the compiler does here anyway.
you're right, cowdata is 64 bits, but string truncate it already. nevermind then

Not too familiar with char types, but given how it's used here, shouldn't `c` be a simple `char` here, removing the need for casting? Why do we use `char32_t` to store `uint8_t`?

Same question below for `get_line()`.

We'd usually do:
```suggestion
			if (num == 0.0) {
```
but I guess you want to explicitly communicate that this shouldn't be simplified to `== 0` or `== 0.0f` or `Math::is_zero_approx(num)` by an overzealous refactorer?
Actually I forgot to remove this review comment, I noticed even `RandomPCG::random()` modified here uses plain `abs()`. It probably doesn't make much difference either way.
That being said I think it's also fine to keep it simple like done in this PR (avoid regressions), and refactor the code for readability in a follow-up.

> This seems to be an expectation in the codebase indeed, which I believe mirrors memcpy?

That is what the codebase implies, but calling memcpy with null parameters is undefined behavior. It makes gcc remove subsequent nullptr checks because calling memcpy on a pointer proves it is not nullptr, because that would be UB.
Yes, I don't know how I missed that, will change.

Yeah, in this case I wanted it to be very clear that this was just and only dealing with the "Exactly 0" case, because otherwise the new code would return it as "0.00000000000000", but for "approximately 0" we don't want that, because if someone wants to serialize an "approximately 0" value, who are we to truncate it?

```suggestion
	ERR_FAIL_NULl_V(p_dst, -1);
```
Now that it's not a compound expression
Ah, you're right, I'll update. I can't believe this didn't make tests fail. 😅
